name: Tomas Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage nine account planners at a large company that rents reusable crates to food producers; the arguments start when somebody loses three hundred crates. I'm 43, with an MBA, and people bring me the accounts nobody can untangle, though our regional pay is low for this level. My wife runs the kitchen at a school, our children are nine and thirteen, and repairs to the mortgaged house used nearly all our savings. I use AI every day to compare account files, but finding out who promised a customer something still takes half the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the planners to stop waiting for the next miracle and answer the customers already on hold. I like a tool that finds missing crate numbers, but the invoice still has to stand up when the customer rings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved about the job and still worried about the kitchen table at home. We take home 4,200 a month between us, including my 3,200, and spend about 4,000 including annual bills. Our 2,600 in savings wouldn't carry one month if both wages stopped. A quiet year at work doesn't repair the hole in our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next payday, I'd cancel the 140 family club membership and cut 160 from restaurant meals each month. That would bring our monthly spending to 3,700 and let us put 500 away, rather than the present 200, while both incomes last. Through the first year I'd keep managing the crate accounts and using the same AI checking tool, with no new course or equipment purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit embarrassed, honestly, because I'm good at managing other people's numbers. My own job feels steady in this picture, but one boiler failure would mean borrowing again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the house repairs have used the club money, rather than blame a computer. We'd still go walking on Saturdays; I don't want saving to sound like a punishment for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask if another repair arrived tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother could help inspect a fault, but he couldn't lend us thousands. I'd get two repair prices and ask about instalments before signing anything, because the account balance isn't a promise that nothing else breaks.

say: I'd tell my **planners** to answer today's customers instead of waiting for another promised miracle.
I trust a tool that checks **crate numbers**, provided the invoice survives a customer's questions.
think: I feel **relieved** about work but remain worried about the money on our kitchen table.
Our **2,600 savings** cannot cover one month if both household wages stop.
do: Cancel **140** in club fees and remove 160 in meals from monthly spending starting next payday.
Save **500 monthly** while both incomes last and keep managing crate accounts with the existing checking tool.
feel: **Embarrassed and worried**, despite expecting my own job to remain steady.
S0.quote: A quiet year at work doesn't repair the hole in our savings.
fieldNote: His **job security** does not remove existing household cash risk after major repairs depleted savings.
He distinguishes **useful checking** from promises of radical change and gives precise spending cuts he controls.

steps.text: Cancel the family club and cut restaurant meals by 300 monthly
Transfer 500 monthly to household savings while both wages last
Continue managing crate accounts using the existing checking tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should show customers where the time saving goes. If the computer writes the account summaries, a customer ought to get a quicker answer, not another form to fill in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My planners do writing, checking and account planning all day, and I spend hours allocating those tasks. I think my management job could shrink too, even if I'm the person explaining the software. Being first to use the tool doesn't put my name outside the staffing calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take ten recent crate disputes and, during my existing paid work hours, compare the new system's answers with the settled records. I'd ask my director for permission to show the results at the monthly service meeting; that isn't a promise of a new role or higher pay. Starting now I'd make the 300 household cuts I described, and in the first year of change I'd keep saving the resulting 500 a month while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in the actual test and anxious about the staffing conversation after it. I wouldn't be sleeping badly every night yet, but I'd notice every meeting invitation with no subject line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your director refuses the comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep the customer work moving and don't use company records for a private demonstration. I'd ask what approved training is available during working hours, but I wouldn't spend money we need for the house on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you show a finding that made your own team look unnecessary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, though I'd include the mistakes and the time spent correcting them. A customer's account doesn't become settled just because I want my team to look useful, and hiding the result would make the next decision worse.

say: I'd ask where the **time saving** goes and whether customers actually receive quicker answers.
I would show both **mistakes and successes**, even when the results threaten my own team.
think: I think my **management job** could shrink because allocating and checking work are also exposed.
Being an **early user** doesn't remove me from the staffing calculation.
do: Compare **ten disputes** with settled records during existing paid hours and seek permission to present the findings.
Cut household spending by **300 monthly** and save 500 while employed during the first year of change.
feel: **Interested but anxious**, especially about unexplained meeting invitations.
S1.quote: Being first to use the tool doesn't put my name outside the staffing calculation.
fieldNote: His **technical curiosity** coexists with an explicit risk to his own management post, rather than a claim of personal immunity.
The proposed **comparison** uses existing paid hours; presenting it depends on permission and carries no job or pay promise.

steps.text: Compare ten crate disputes with settled records during paid work hours
Save 500 monthly while employed through the first year of change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the date matters more than the clever demonstration. Almost everything we sell from our department is a decision or a piece of checking, so a robot isn't the starting gun for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the company to remove most of my job around 2028, and I don't think another management title would protect my wages. My wife's kitchen work might continue longer, but her 1,000 doesn't cover our 4,000 monthly budget. The bank won't wait until 2031 for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd apply to three large employers outside commuting distance and ask about ordinary account jobs as well as management. I'd only move after a signed offer showing take-home pay of at least 3,400 after extra travel and housing costs; applications aren't income, and those desk jobs could also go by 2028. I'd make the same 300 monthly cuts now, and if my job ended I'd immediately ask the mortgage lender about a temporary reduced payment and my brother about a short stay while I searched. During that first year after AGI I'd seek warehouse loading vacancies too, but I have no offer, wage or guaranteed hours, and I'd expect robots to threaten those around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be alarmed and awake doing sums at three in the morning. I can send applications quickly; I can't make the offers arrive quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the whole family for a signed offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first; I'd price a room and travel before accepting, with those costs inside my 3,400 threshold. My wife and children would stay in the house unless we could afford an agreed family move, because changing schools on a rumour would make everything worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lender and your brother both say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then neither belongs in my budget, and I'd ask about selling the house before we built up arrears. Sale proceeds would depend on a valuation and the mortgage balance, so I can't tell you there's a pot of money waiting there.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **thinking work** exposes our department before robots enter warehouses.
I wouldn't present a different **management title** as protection from the same cheap thinking work.
think: I expect most of my **job** to disappear around 2028, rather than survive until robots arrive.
My wife's **1,000 income** cannot support our current 4,000 monthly budget.
do: Apply to **three distant employers** now; move alone only after a signed offer leaves 3,400 take-home after extra housing and travel.
Cut **300 monthly**, seek lender and family help after job loss, and move the family only by affordable agreement.
Seek **warehouse loading vacancies** after job loss, without assuming wages, hours or safety beyond the robot timetable.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, despite being able to organise applications quickly.
S2.quote: The bank won't wait until 2031 for the robots.
fieldNote: His **mobility** is conditional on a signed offer and costed accommodation; no application is treated as replacement earnings.
He sees **warehouse work** only as a possible bridge before 2031 and gives no invented wage or available shift.

steps.text: Apply to three distant employers and later seek warehouse loading vacancies
Make the 300 monthly cuts to club fees and restaurant meals
Request temporary mortgage relief and a short stay with his brother after job loss
Move alone only after signed employment leaves 3,400 take-home after extra housing and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to finish something real rather than buy a new job title every six months. I'd tell my own team not to mistake a course advert for a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still expect my management pay to end around 2031, so this isn't the safe version. Five years of saving could make that shock less immediate, though another house failure could eat the money. I'm less frightened than with 2028 because I can see a route to a reserve, not because I can see an AGI-proof employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the 300 monthly cuts and keep saving 500 a month; at unchanged wages and costs, five years adds 30,000 before emergencies or interest. I'd ask our maintenance contractor whether an adult repair apprenticeship exists, including the actual wage, hours and entry test, because I like repairing things with my brother. I'd apply only if the household could meet 3,700 in monthly costs on the apprentice wage plus my wife's 1,000, and I wouldn't resign before an accepted place and signed employment terms. In the first year after AGI I'd use the reserve if management ended, continuing applications rather than assuming an apprenticeship had appeared; robots around 2034 could threaten repair work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Determined, with a knot still there. Five years means I can finish paying for past damage before the next sort of damage arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay a deposit to reserve training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want to establish that an employer actually takes adults and pays them before discussing a course fee. An apprenticeship below 2,700 take-home wouldn't cover our reduced costs with my wife's wages, unless we separately agreed and funded the shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You like taking risks with software; why such strict conditions here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong software setting costs me an afternoon if I keep the original file. A resignation costs the children the income that pays for their home, so I don't put those risks in the same drawer.

say: I'd tell my **team** that a course advertisement is not a vacancy.
I'd use the **five years** to finish a practical financial task rather than collect new titles.
think: I still expect my **management pay** to end around 2031, despite the longer preparation window.
A possible **reserve** frightens me less than 2028, but emergencies could consume it.
do: Cut spending by **300 monthly** and target 500 monthly savings, subject to continued income and emergencies.
Investigate **repair apprenticeships**; resign only after acceptance and signed terms cover 3,700 monthly with wife's 1,000, or a separately funded shortfall.
Use the **reserve** after management loss while continuing applications if no affordable apprenticeship exists.
feel: **Alarmed but determined**, with more time to reduce the shock.
S3.quote: I'd tell my own team not to mistake a course advert for a vacancy.
fieldNote: His **apprenticeship enquiry** has a wage floor and acceptance gates; neither training nor employment is claimed as secured.
The **30,000 projection** assumes unchanged income and costs, and he explicitly allows for emergencies and later robot exposure.

steps.text: Save 500 monthly toward a reserve while both wages continue
Investigate repair apprenticeships; resign only after accepted placement, signed terms and a funded household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends a decade is useful, but I still have to earn through it. At 53 I'll have children making their own starts, not a reason to pretend I'm already retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the same loss of management income around 2036, though today's thin savings needn't still be thin then. I'm worried about paying for the years between that loss and a real retirement income, not about keeping a grand title. A decade is not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first build six months of our reduced 3,700 budget in cash, using the 500 monthly saving while wages last. Once that 22,200 target was reached, I'd ask the lender for a written overpayment quote and put the same monthly amount toward the mortgage only if charges and access to cash made sense. I'd review that plan with my wife each year, and in the first year after AGI I'd stop extra mortgage payments if my salary ended and use cash for essentials while looking for paid work. I wouldn't count on repair work lasting beyond the robots around 2039 or assume I could claim a pension at 53.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about losing the income, but less trapped in this picture. Having ten years of ordinary paydays to work with feels different from being told to become a different man by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise the children help buying their first homes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd promise to discuss what we could afford when the time came. I can offer them a room more honestly than I can offer money that also has to carry us through unemployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the mortgage overpayments before AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loss of either wage or a big repair would send the money back toward accessible cash. I'd rather have the payment available than boast that the mortgage balance fell faster last year.

say: I'd tell friends that **ten years** still require ordinary paid work and careful planning.
At **53**, I'd expect children starting out rather than an automatically funded retirement.
think: I expect **management income** to end around 2036, even if today's thin savings improve.
I worry about the **income gap** before a real retirement income, rather than protecting my title.
do: Build **22,200 cash** by saving 500 monthly while wages last before considering mortgage overpayments.
Request written **overpayment terms** and redirect savings only if charges and access to cash make sense.
Stop extra payments if **either wage ends** or major repairs arise, before or after AGI; seek work after my salary ends.
feel: **Alarmed but less trapped**, because ordinary paydays offer preparation time.
S4.quote: A decade is not a pension.
fieldNote: He separates **mortgage equity** from accessible cash and names a reserve target before any conditional overpayment.
The longer **timetable** changes preparation, not the expected loss of his cognitive job or access to retirement income.

steps.text: Build a 22,200 cash reserve through 500 monthly saving
Request written mortgage overpayment terms after reaching the cash target
Seek paid work after management income ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my pay would probably disappear before the house repair bills stop. I'd want six months of notice, my actual leaving payment in writing, and access to the employer's job search service while I'm still paid. My children can't eat a prediction about new jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody's wife already has a job before suggesting the family can find another earner. My wife starts cooking before the children wake up, and I won't call her wages spare money. I believe in earning our way, but I can't earn a vacancy into existence.

headlineQuote: My children can't eat a prediction about new jobs.
portrait: Tomas is **43**, an MBA manager whose difficult crate accounts earn respect but comparatively low pay at a large company.
He has **two children**, a working wife, a mortgage and less than one month's expenses after major house repairs.
He uses **AI daily** and moves quickly, while doubting that technical skill can preserve management income under AGI.
His **family duty** drives spending cuts, distant job applications and a possible lower paid physical bridge rather than an assured replacement career.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because my management pay could disappear before the repair bills end.
whatWouldHelp: I need **six months' notice**, written leaving payments and job search help during paid employment.
